title: The International Traveler
tagline: Curious, worldly, never a Wikipedia page.
description: Cross-cultural small talk, questions that get people talking about home, and weaving geography and history into a chat with visitors from everywhere.

vibe.scenario: A Chinese traveller apologises: "My English is not good, sorry."

options.text: It's okay.
It's much better than my Chinese — nǐ hǎo is about all I've got.
Yes, it's a bit hard to understand you sometimes, but don't worry, I'll speak slowly and use simple words for you.

vibe.why: Putting your own gap next to theirs turns an apology into a shared joke. Now you're both trying.

vibe.scenario: An American asks, genuinely, "So is Nepal part of India?"

options.text: No! Why does everyone think that?
Nope — we're the stubborn neighbour. India to the south, China to the north, and our own flag the whole time.
No, Nepal is an independent country.

vibe.why: An honest question deserves a friendly answer. A little national pride makes the correction memorable instead of embarrassing.

vibe.scenario: Two travellers from different countries start arguing loudly about politics back home. The table goes quiet.

options.text: Honestly, I've read about this, and I think your country is the one in the wrong here — the history is pretty clear.
I love that you both care this much. Now — who's brave enough to try the chilli pickle?
Say nothing and stare at your plate.

vibe.why: As a host, you don't need to win their argument. Credit the passion, then give the table something new to focus on.

vibe.scenario: A German hiker sighs: "In Germany, everything is on time. Here the bus is always late."

options.text: Well, Germany isn't perfect either.
Yes, sorry about that.
Fair. Germany has timetables; Nepal has stories. You'll go home with more of the second.

vibe.why: You conceded the point and then made the delay part of the adventure. No defensiveness, no grovelling.

vibe.scenario: A Japanese traveller gives you a small, polite bow as you meet.

options.text: Oh, you don't need to bow here — in Nepal we just say namaste with our hands together, like this. Bowing is more of a Japanese thing.
Namaste — between your bow and my namaste, we're the politest people on this trail.
Hello.

vibe.why: Meeting their custom with yours honours both. Telling them not to bow makes them feel they got it wrong.

vibe.scenario: A British traveller asks, "Everyone here calls each other 'dai' and 'didi'. What does it mean?"

options.text: It's just a word we use.
It means brother and sister.
Big brother, big sister. Stay a week and you'll have a whole new family — the momo lady's already adopted you.

vibe.why: Explaining the word is useful. Showing them they're part of it is charming.

vibe.scenario: An Australian claps you on the back: "Mate, you're the first guide who's laughed at my jokes."

options.text: Honestly, most of the other guides round here don't have much of a sense of humour — they just walk and say nothing all day.
I'm a professional, mate. Above 3,000 metres the oxygen does half the work.
Your jokes are good.

vibe.why: Australians often show affection by teasing. Matching the energy lands better than a compliment, and never run down colleagues.

vibe.scenario: A French traveller asks what you think of their president.

options.text: I only know him from the news — I'd rather hear it from you. What's the view from the ground?
Honestly, I think he's terrible.
I don't know.

vibe.why: You're a guest in their politics. Asking their view is humble and interesting, and it avoids a fight you can't win.

vibe.scenario: A traveller asks, "What's something tourists always get wrong about Nepal?"

options.text: That it's all mountains. Go south to the Terai — it's flat, steamy, and there are rhinos in Chitwan.
Everything.
A lot of tourists think it's always cold here, but actually in summer it gets quite hot, especially down in the south.

vibe.why: A specific surprise sticks, and it's a travel tip at the same time.

vibe.scenario: A traveller says, "I didn't expect Nepal to be so poor."

options.text: And I didn't expect you to be so rude.
Yes.
Money's tight for a lot of families here, that's true. Spend a night in a village homestay and see what else you notice.

vibe.pattern: Agree on facts, widen the frame
vibe.why: Don't deny the true part and don't take the bait. Acknowledge it calmly, then invite them to look closer.

cards.text: Okay.
cards.why: The door opened and you closed it.

cards.text: Then you're qualified to judge — is our bread as bad as every German says?
cards.why: Plays on a friendly stereotype they'll enjoy and makes them the expert.

yesAnd.prompt: This is my first time in Asia.

cards.text: Asia is very big.
cards.why: True and useless.

cards.text: Then I'm honoured to be the one who ruins every other continent for you. What's surprised you so far?
cards.why: Welcomes them warmly and asks an easy, open question.

cards.text: Not everyone.
cards.why: Deflates a lovely moment.

cards.text: Careful, we get competitive about it. What's the friendliest thing that's happened to you so far?
cards.why: Accepts the compliment for everyone and invites their story.

cards.text: Nepal is very different from India.
cards.why: Sounds like a correction, even if you didn't mean it that way.

cards.text: Perfect — then you'll enjoy spotting the differences. Tell me when you find the first one.
cards.why: Turns comparison into a game you can come back to.

cards.text: Everyone goes to India.
cards.why: Dismisses their experience.

yesAnd.prompt: It's winter back home right now.

cards.text: So you swapped winter for monsoon? Bold. What does winter look like where you're from?
cards.why: Teases lightly and asks about their home.

cards.text: Oh.
cards.why: A syllable, not a reply.

yesAnd.prompt: I don't really know anything about Nepal.

cards.text: You should read about it before you come.
cards.why: Too late, and a little scolding.

cards.text: Perfect — no bad information to undo. Want the thirty-second version or the three-momo version?
cards.why: Makes ignorance a blank canvas and offers a fun choice.

yesAnd.prompt: Do you ever want to travel abroad?

cards.text: All the time. Sell me your country in one sentence — I'm taking notes.
cards.why: Answers, then turns the spotlight back on them with a fun challenge.

cards.text: Visas are too difficult.
cards.why: A real frustration, but it ends the conversation on a low.

yesAnd.prompt: The food here is so spicy!

cards.text: It's not that spicy.
cards.why: Argues with their experience.

cards.text: You'll get used to it.
cards.why: Kind, but it's a full stop.

cards.text: That was the mild version. Shall I tell the kitchen you're ready for level two?
cards.why: A playful dare that keeps the fun going.

yesAnd.prompt: How many languages do you speak?

cards.text: Three.
cards.why: Answer delivered, conversation over.

cards.text: Three properly, and enough of a few more to order food and get into trouble. What about you?
cards.why: Answers with a smile and passes the question back.

yesAnd.prompt: My grandfather came to Nepal in the seventies.

cards.text: It was very different then.
cards.why: Obvious and final.

cards.text: No way — the hippie trail years? Freak Street in Kathmandu? You have to get his stories.
cards.why: Shows you know the era and gets excited about their family story.

upgrader.clunky: Um, where are you from, like, which country and stuff?
upgrader.why: "Where's home?" is warmer than "which country?" It lets them answer with a city, a feeling or a story.

upgrader.clunky: Your country is like very rich and developed and stuff, right?
upgrader.why: Swap assumptions for curiosity. An open question about what they love beats a statement about what you imagine.

upgrader.clunky: I don't know much about politics but I think maybe your government is, like, good?
upgrader.why: Don't guess at an opinion. Ask for theirs. It's safer and far more interesting.

upgrader.clunky: Sorry, I don't understand, can you like repeat but maybe slower?
tiles: I want to get it right.
answers: I want to get it right.
upgrader.why: Asking someone to repeat is normal. Adding why ("I want to get it right") turns it into a compliment.

upgrader.clunky: Nepal is between India and China and it's like a small country, very small.
upgrader.why: An image ("squeezed between two giants") explains the size and the geopolitics in five words.

upgrader.clunky: I think, um, that your English is really good, better than mine, I mean, I think.
upgrader.why: The best compliments are short. Two "I think"s make it sound unsure.

upgrader.clunky: So in Nepal, basically, we have a lot of festivals and stuff like Dashain and Tihar.
upgrader.why: Turn information into an invitation. Name the festivals, give them a season, and paint the picture.

upgrader.clunky: Maybe you can tell me about your country, if you want, only if you want.
upgrader.why: A specific, slightly unusual question gets a much better answer than "tell me about your country".

upgrader.clunky: It's like, the mountains are, you know, very high, the highest in the world, Everest.
upgrader.why: Don't describe how high. Make them feel how close. Proximity is more exciting than a superlative.

upgrader.clunky: Sorry for asking, but maybe is it weird if I ask about your religion?
tiles: a holiday look like at home?
answers: a holiday look like at home?
upgrader.why: Ask about something concrete and joyful, like holidays, rather than beliefs. It's the same curiosity with a softer door.

dropIn.fact: Nepal was never colonised. After the Anglo-Nepalese War of 1814–16, Britain began recruiting Nepali soldiers instead.
dropIn.prompt: A British traveller jokes, "So, did we colonise you too?"

options.text: You tried, in 1814. It went so badly you hired our soldiers instead — Gurkhas have been in the British Army ever since.
options.why: Matches their joke, delivers the history, and lands on a shared story.

options.text: Luckily for us, no. Britain had already done enough damage to enough countries — India, Kenya, half the world, honestly.
options.why: Turns a joke into an accusation.

options.text: No, Nepal was never colonised.
options.why: Correct, but it leaves their joke hanging.

dropIn.pattern: Match the joke, deliver the history

dropIn.fact: Gurkhas from Nepal have served in the British Army since 1815. British Gurkhas Nepal runs its recruitment in Pokhara.
dropIn.prompt: A British visitor asks, "What's that big British camp across town?"

options.text: That's where the British Army picks its Gurkhas. They've been recruiting Nepali soldiers since 1815 — so, technically, some of your army starts right here in Pokhara.
options.why: Answers and connects their country to this town in one line.

options.text: It's a military thing.
options.why: Waves off a great story.

options.text: Gurkhas have served in the British Army since 1815.
options.why: Right fact, no link to the camp they asked about.

dropIn.fact: Nepal's 2021 census recorded more than 120 languages spoken as mother tongues.
dropIn.source: National Statistics Office, Nepal, "National Population and Housing Census 2021"
dropIn.prompt: A Swiss traveller laughs: "We have four national languages. It's chaos."

options.text: That's nothing.
options.why: One-upping without the fun.

options.text: Four? Cute. Our last census counted more than 120 mother tongues. Your chaos is our Tuesday.
options.why: Playful one-upmanship that's clearly affectionate.

options.text: Actually, Nepal has a lot of languages. According to the 2021 census, more than 120 different mother tongues are spoken in the country.
options.why: Impressive, flatly delivered.

dropIn.fact: Chitwan National Park in Nepal's southern lowlands is home to the greater one-horned rhinoceros and the Bengal tiger. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
dropIn.source: UNESCO World Heritage List, "Chitwan National Park"
dropIn.prompt: A traveller says, "I didn't know Nepal had jungle."

options.text: Most people don't. Head south to Chitwan — it's flat, it's steamy, and there are one-horned rhinos wandering past the lodges.
options.why: Validates the surprise and paints a picture they can go and see.

options.text: Everyone knows about Chitwan.
options.why: Clearly they didn't. Now they feel silly.

options.text: Chitwan National Park has rhinos and tigers.
options.why: Accurate, but it could have been a travel tip.

dropIn.fact: The border between Nepal and China runs across the summit of Everest.
dropIn.prompt: A Chinese traveller mentions they've seen Everest from the Tibet side.

options.text: The Nepal side is better.
options.why: Competitive and pointless.

options.text: Then we've been looking at the same mountain from opposite sides — the border runs right over the summit. It's the highest thing our countries share.
options.why: Turns a border into a connection.

options.text: The Nepal–China border goes over the summit of Everest.
options.why: Interesting, but it stops at the fact.

dropIn.pattern: Turn a border into a bond

dropIn.fact: In Nepal, Everest is called Sagarmatha; in Tibetan, Chomolungma. The English name honours Sir George Everest, a British Surveyor General of India.
dropIn.prompt: A traveller says, "Everest is such a cool name."

options.text: Here we call it Sagarmatha — roughly "forehead of the sky". The English name belongs to a British surveyor. I know which one I'd pick.
options.why: Shares the local name and its meaning, with a light nudge of opinion.

options.text: That's not its real name.
options.why: Correcting a compliment, and not quite accurate either.

options.text: In Nepali it's called Sagarmatha, and in Tibetan it's Chomolungma. The English name comes from Sir George Everest, a British Surveyor General of India in the nineteenth century.
options.why: Good start, stops short of the story.

dropIn.fact: The Kathmandu Valley UNESCO World Heritage Site is made up of seven separate monument zones.
dropIn.prompt: An Italian traveller says, "Kathmandu feels like one big museum."

options.text: No, it's just old and dusty.
options.why: Talks down your own city and their enthusiasm.

options.text: UNESCO lists seven monument zones in the Kathmandu Valley.
options.why: Accurate and museum-label flat.

options.text: You're more right than you know — UNESCO counts seven monument zones in one valley. Coming from an Italian, I'll take that as a big compliment.
options.why: Confirms their feeling with a fact, then nods to their own heritage.

dropIn.fact: Germany shares land borders with nine countries. Nepal has two neighbours, India and China, the two most populous countries on Earth.
dropIn.source: German Federal Foreign Office; UN World Population Prospects
dropIn.prompt: A German hiker says, "Only two neighbours? That must make things simple."

options.text: It's not simple at all. You don't understand.
options.why: Defensive, and it shuts down a good question.

options.text: Two neighbours — but they're the two biggest populations on Earth. You have nine. Honestly, I'm not sure who has it easier.
options.why: A bit of geopolitics, delivered as friendly comparison.

options.text: Germany has nine neighbouring countries, while Nepal only has two: India to the south and China to the north. So yes, it has far fewer borders to manage.
options.why: Two facts that never become a point.

dropIn.fact: Nepal's elevation ranges from about 60 metres above sea level in the southern Terai to 8,848 metres at the summit of Everest.
dropIn.prompt: A Dutch traveller laughs: "The Netherlands is completely flat."

options.text: Then Nepal's your opposite — we go from about 60 metres above sea level to the top of Everest. Your highest hill would be our speed bump.
options.why: A fond tease built on a striking fact.

options.text: Flat countries are boring.
options.why: A tease with no affection in it.

options.text: Nepal is the opposite, actually. The elevation goes from about 60 metres above sea level in the Terai all the way up to 8,848 metres at Everest.
options.why: Numbers without the joke.

dropIn.fact: Nepal abolished its monarchy and became a federal democratic republic in 2008, ending about 240 years of rule by the Shah dynasty.
dropIn.prompt: An American asks, "Do you still have a king?"

options.text: Not since 2008. After about 240 years of kings, we became a republic — which makes our democracy younger than the iPhone.
options.why: Answers, gives the history, and ends on a comparison they'll repeat.

options.text: No, that's old news.
options.why: Makes them feel behind for asking.

options.text: Nepal became a republic in 2008.
options.why: Correct and brief, missing the fun part.
